With a 25bp hike close to fully priced, the reaction is likely to hinge on the statement and Governor Bullock's press conference, in particular whether the board keeps November open. title: Weak Treasury auctions and Fed hike bets push US 10-year yield to highest since June 2007
body: Yields at these levels tighten financial conditions across mortgages, corporate debt and equity valuations, and analysts have said a sustained move above 5.2% would likely keep the US dollar supported while pressuring gold and risk assets. The S&P 500 has so far held within a few percent of its record high, so a further rise in real yields is a test of that resilience. Borrowing costs are already feeling it, with the average 30-year US mortgage rate at around 7.1%, its highest in more than two years. Oil has rebounded on Iran headlines, but the message from the bond market is that supply and Fed policy, not energy, are now the dominant drivers. --- Treasury yields are climbing on real yields and weak auction demand rather than inflation expectations, leaving the 10-year above 5.2% as markets price a likely October Fed hike. Summary: The US 10-year Treasury yield rose above 5.2% on Monday, its highest since June 2007, while the 30-year yield has reached around 5.5%, its highest since 2004. A senior US economist at Aberdeen said the rise is driven by real yields rather than inflation expectations, noting the two-year breakeven has barely moved this week and remains well below earlier highs. The economist said markets are reacting to weak Treasury auction demand and signs of an accelerating US economy, which are raising expectations of tighter Fed policy.

title: More from Araqchi: Iran hopes for final US reply via Qatar by Tuesday
body: The reference to a Tuesday timeline gives oil traders a near-term catalyst, which concentrates headline risk into the next day or so. Language that mediation has become more serious is modestly constructive for those pricing a Hormuz reopening, though Tehran has not detailed its conditions and Washington has publicly disputed the idea of sanctions relief, so the signal is mixed. Crude has been trading in both directions on each diplomatic headline, and that is likely to continue until a US reply either narrows or widens the gaps on sequencing. --- Earlier: Araqchi: Iran discussed ideas with Qatari mediators, Hormuz conditions must be met Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief, calls Axios report a hoax ---Iran says mediation through Qatar and Pakistan has turned more serious since it presented a plan, and it wants the US final answer by Tuesday. Summary: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said he hopes to receive the US final response through Qatari mediators by Tuesday, according to IRNA. He said Tehran discussed with the Qatari mediators ideas on how to fulfil Iran's conditions, and that the mediators will raise those ideas with the US side. Araqchi said the Qatari and Pakistani mediation channels have taken a more serious form after Iran presented a plan. The remarks follow earlier comments that the US response will be relayed through Qatar and that the Supreme Leader's conditions must be implemented for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen.

body: The remarks suggest the Qatari mediation channel is live, but they also show Iran tying any Hormuz reopening to conditions it has not spelled out, which keeps a supply risk premium in oil. title: Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief, calls Axios report a hoax
body: The denial adds another layer of uncertainty to a crude market that has been trading almost entirely on Iran diplomacy headlines. Market reports noted that the original relief reports coincided with softer oil, a slightly weaker US dollar and gains in Treasuries, equities and gold, so a flat denial risks unwinding some of that repricing. The counterweight is that price reactions to Trump's social media posts on the war have been shrinking, according to Axios reporting in August, which may limit the move. For oil, the direction of travel still depends on whether mediated talks make progress on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and on whether conflicting official messaging keeps a risk premium in the market. --- Trump's flat denial leaves markets with conflicting signals on Iran sanctions relief just as mediators prepare to bring both sides back to the table. Summary: Trump posted on Truth Social that an Axios story saying he offered Iran sanctions relief and frozen funds was untrue, saying he offered "nothing," and demanded that Axios withdraw it immediately. Axios, citing US officials, had reported that Trump is willing to provide sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds in return for concrete Iranian steps on the nuclear program. CNN carried similar remarks from a US official.

title: Oil Rises as US-Iran Uncertainty Persists
body: Crude oil rose above $93 per barrel on Tuesday, extending its recent gains as persistent uncertainty over US-Iran negotiations outweighed the impact of resumed flows through Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline. Iranian officials have reportedly downplayed the likelihood of a deal to end hostilities in the Middle East and reopen the Strait of Hormuz before the US midterm elections in November. Recent talks between the US and Iran in New York yielded limited progress, with President Donald Trump rejecting Tehran's latest proposal to reopen the strategic shipping lane. Even so, Trump is said to be weighing potential sanctions relief for Iran and the unfreezing of assets if there is meaningful movement toward a new nuclear agreement. At the same time, Saudi Arabia has reportedly restored oil flows to about 3.5 million barrels per day after repairing a key pipeline that offers an alternative export route bypassing Hormuz. title: UK Shop Price Inflation Slows in September
body: UK shop price inflation eased to 1.4% year-on-year in September 2026, down from 1.5% in August and slightly below market expectations of 1.5%. Despite the slowdown, it remained above the three-month average of 1.3%. Food price inflation fell to 2.5% from 2.8%, supported by promotions that reduced the cost of meat and dairy. However, poor harvests in Europe pushed up fruit prices, while elevated commodity costs kept chocolate and confectionery prices high. Non-food inflation also edged down, slipping to 0.8% from 0.9%, as heavy discounting lowered the prices of back-to-school essentials. The British Retail Consortium noted that retailers are continuing to absorb higher business rates, employment costs, energy bills and packaging taxes, but cautioned that there is a limit to how much additional cost pressure businesses can bear. In contrast, the UK's broader CPI inflation rate rose to 3.1% in August and is projected to exceed 4% in early 2027, driven by higher energy prices linked to the war in Iran. body: Annual shop price inflation in the United Kingdom edged down in September 2026, with the BRC Shop Price Index easing to 1.4% year-over-year from 1.5% in the previous month. The latest reading, updated on 28 September 2026, signals a further moderation in price pressures on the high street. The index measures the year-over-year change in shop prices, comparing the price level in September 2026 with that of September 2025. The prior figure compared August 2026 prices with those of August 2025. The slight deceleration suggests that while prices are still rising compared with a year earlier, the pace of increase continues to cool, offering some relief to consumers and potentially easing pressure on retailers navigating a still-cautious spending environment. Analysts and market participants will be watching subsequent releases closely to assess whether September's decline marks the start of a broader downtrend in sentiment or a short-term pullback within an otherwise stable confidence environment. title: New Zealand Stocks Track Wall Street Lower
body: The NZX 50 slipped 76 points, or 0.6%, to 13,755 in Tuesday morning trade, snapping the gains made in the previous session and mirroring an overnight decline on Wall Street. The drop followed a jump in US Treasury yields, as rising oil prices rekindled inflation concerns and strengthened expectations of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike. Investors were also positioning ahead of a series of key data releases this week, including New Zealand's September business confidence figures, China's PMI data, and the US PCE Index and labour market reports, all of which could influence the Fed's policy stance at its upcoming meeting. The benchmark index fell to its lowest level since 18 September, with energy, real estate, and utilities shares exerting the most downward pressure. title: Jamaica Raises Policy Rate to 6%
body: At its September 2026 meeting, Jamaica's central bank raised its policy rate by 50 basis points to 6.0%, responding to persistent inflationary pressures, higher commodity prices, and elevated geopolitical risks that are clouding the economic outlook. The bank emphasized that inflation risks remain tilted to the upside. Headline inflation rose to 7.9% in August from 7.5% in July, staying above the target range for a third straight month, while core inflation was unchanged at 5.2%. Policymakers expect inflation to increase further in the near term before gradually returning to the target range by mid-2027. Drought conditions and a strengthening El Niño are projected to keep agricultural prices high, and rising global commodity prices are feeding through to higher fuel, energy, and transport costs. In addition, post-disaster recovery spending following Hurricane Melissa could further add to price pressures. Businesses' 12‑month inflation expectations climbed to 7.3% in July from 6.7% in June. Overall, the manufacturing Composite Business Sentiment Index fell by 4.3 points to 99.5 in September, and the outlook index for the following month declined by 1.4 points to 101.1, both reflecting a worsening in business sentiment. title: Japan's Katayama says undervalued yen is problematic, agrees with Bessent on cooperation
body: The yen is the main read-through. Katayama's line that an undervalued yen is problematic, paired with her promise of close US Treasury contact, adds to verbal pressure on USD/JPY (around 157 in recent sessions) after August's joint intervention. Her denial that the government is reflationary and her stress on market-set rates may offer a little support to the yen and to JGB sentiment, but with no level or action mentioned, traders are likely to keep testing officials' resolve. --- Katayama kept to the familiar script of cooperation and communication, but her view that an undervalued yen is problematic keeps the pressure on USD/JPY. Summary Katayama said Japan and the US agreed to step up cooperation, when asked about her September 25 phone talks with Treasury Secretary Bessent. She said Japan will keep close communication with the US Treasury to help ensure orderly foreign exchange markets. She said an undervalued yen, in general, is problematic. She said Prime Minister Takaichi's administration is not reflationary and that interest rates are determined by markets. She said the ministry will communicate closely with bond market participants and conduct appropriate debt management policy. She said it will stay in close touch with market participants while maintaining a high sense of urgency. title: ICYMI: Senate report says Iran relied on Tether's USDT to bypass sanctions, WSJ reports
body: The report is an allegation from one party's investigators, and it does not announce any action, so the direct market effect is likely to be limited to headline risk around USDT and other stablecoin issuers. Tether's roughly 60% share of the stablecoin market means any move by US officials to force faster freezes could matter for crypto liquidity more than for the token's peg. The oil angle is the one to watch: the report ties Iran's use of the token to continued oil sales to allies such as China, so tighter enforcement on those payment channels could add to supply friction at a time when Brent is trading near $105. --- Yesterday: Tether's $84 million question: whose money did the US actually seize? --- Senate Democrats say Tether's dollar-pegged token has become a core sanctions-dodging tool for Iran, although blockchain data suggests Tehran's reliance may be easing. The report analysed around 850 wallets sanctioned by the US and Israel over Iran links and found 84% transacted exclusively, or near exclusively, in USDT. title: State Street: Gold may test $4,000 on rate fears but $5,000 still possible in six months
body: Gold is trading as a rates and dollar story for now, with futures sliding to their lowest since early August on Monday as Iran headlines, higher oil and Fed hike odds above 70% for October lifted yields. That keeps the $4,000 area in focus as a psychological floor, and a break below it would test the idea that structural demand can offset a hawkish Fed. Any pullback in real yields or the dollar, for example after payrolls or a softer inflation print, is the most likely trigger for a rebound. State Street sees gold's slide towards $4,000 as a rates-driven wobble, with China, ETF buyers and fiscal worries still pointing towards $5,000. Summary: State Street Investment Management's head of gold strategy told Kitco that rising rate expectations and surging bond yields could push gold back towards $4,000 an ounce within the next week, but that he expects that floor to hold. He still sees $5,000 as reachable within six months, though a couple more Fed hikes make the path more challenging because of high real yields. Markets have priced in two additional Fed hikes since mid-August, and gold is reacting to peak market hawkishness, with higher nominal and real yields and a stronger dollar. State Street's September report says term premia in the US, UK, France and Germany are at their highest since 2011, with US public debt passing $40 trillion in August.

title: Anthropic IPO prospectus shows $42 billion 2025 loss and $518 billion spending plans
body: A listing at the reported scale would set the first public-market benchmark for a pure-play AI lab, so the prospectus numbers are likely to be read across AI and chip stocks, which have sold off recently. The SpaceX debut gives investors a reference for how a mega-IPO trades after pricing, and a large new supply of AI equity, followed by a possible OpenAI listing, could weigh on existing AI names if appetite for the trade fades. The reported delay until after the midterms leaves time for rates, AI sentiment and the compute spending debate to shift before any pricing. Anthropic's prospectus pairs a 12-fold revenue jump with huge losses and half a trillion dollars of compute commitments, setting up a listing that would test how Wall Street prices AI. --- Earlier: OpenAI scraps GPT-6.1 Astra release over safety concerns, WSJ reports --- Summary: Anthropic's IPO prospectus, seen by Reuters, shows a net loss of $42 billion in 2025 and plans to spend $518 billion on cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations in coming years. Revenue grew 12-fold in 2025 to nearly $4.6 billion, while the operating loss widened to around $8 billion from around $3 billion in 2024. title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.7177 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: UK shop price inflation slows to 1.4% in September as BRC urges business rates help

A budget that eases business rates would offer retailers some relief, but it would not remove the wider energy-driven cost pressure. --- Shop price inflation eased again in September, but retailers say they are close to their limit as war-driven costs mount and the budget approaches. Summary: Annual UK shop price inflation slowed to 1.4% in September from 1.5% in August, a little above the three-month average of 1.3%, according to the British Retail Consortium. Food inflation eased to 2.5% from 2.8% as promotions cut meat and dairy prices, although poor European harvests lifted fruit prices and high commodity prices kept chocolate and confectionery elevated. Non-food inflation slowed to 0.8% from 0.9% as heavy discounting lowered the cost of back-to-school essentials. The BRC's chief executive said retailers have absorbed successive cost increases and cited higher business rates in April, rising employment costs, energy bills and packaging taxes. title: Flatter US yield curve explained: tighter Fed policy, but not an automatic recession call
body: The curve is now a live read on how the market is weighing Fed tightening against heavy Treasury supply, so moves in the 2s10s gap are likely to be treated as a headline signal for rate-sensitive assets. Higher short-end yields tend to keep the US dollar supported, while equities have so far shown resilience despite Treasury yields near their highest since 2007, which leaves them exposed if hike pricing keeps building. Oil is a background driver, because a rebound in crude adds to the case for tighter policy, so Iran headlines can shift rate expectations quickly. The curve is flattening because markets expect a tighter Fed, and UBS argues that signals tighter policy rather than recession, unless jobs, earnings and credit start to weaken. Summary: The gap between 10-year and 2-year Treasury yields has narrowed to just under 30 basis points, with bear flattening accelerating since the Fed raised rates this month and markets pricing at least three more quarter-point hikes over the coming year. UBS says a flatter or inverted curve shows policy is becoming more restrictive, not that recession is certain. It cites Bloomberg data putting the average lead before recession at around 15 months since 1978, with a range of six months to two years, and notes the 2022 inversions were not followed by the expected downturn.

The supply picture is further strained by intense competition for LNG cargoes from Asian buyers and by ongoing maintenance on Norway's gas infrastructure, a crucial source of pipeline gas for Europe. With the heating season approaching, the combination of low inventories and persistent uncertainty over Gulf supplies is leaving the market exposed to renewed bouts of price volatility.
